english: I do not doubt that until now our dispute has been regarded as concerning an obscure question rather than the heart of the faith. People living far from spiritual pursuits are moved only by passing breezes of rumor. Fearing the hostility of the times and lacking the protection of verified truth—as commonly happens amid alarm, when people trust no one less than themselves—they think the more crowded road the safer one.

At present this happens for two reasons: the Manichaeans’ position has won approval in councils of wrongdoing, and the storms of persecution that have been stirred up frighten feeble spirits away from favoring truth.

Thus one group caters both to pleasure and to fear. Its indulgence travels with the crowds of the arena, circus, or theater, seeking to excuse every disgrace by necessity, which always lightens the blame for what was done, and to avoid the world’s uproar by abandoning its principles. These are the things that win a larger following for the defense of vices. Yet most of that crowd, as I said before, believed that advocates of inherited sin and catholics agreed at least in their account of God.

But both in the earlier dispute and in the present one, Augustine’s argument has made clear that the god of those who teach inherited sin is not the God whom Christians, with one voice, worship as just and as the creator of all things. I already anticipate in my mind that many even of those who fell through blind error will correct themselves once they recognize this.

Against us, Mani believes mortals are driven by nature into shameful acts and crimes. He supposes the origin of darkness supplied the material both for bodies and for crimes; that sexual pleasure is the corruption of the human race, the vindication of the devil’s claim, and the force driving people into every dishonor. The advocate of inherited sin follows him in every way, as his heir and offspring, repeatedly proclaiming natural crimes, an eternal necessity of evil arising from dark nothingness, and an affection assigned to the senses that pollutes all the saints and places God’s image in the devil’s kingdom (Genesis 1:26–27).

They now hurl their accusing weapons at God himself, reaching the same conclusion from different beginnings. Mani says: God is good and does no evil. But he adds that God consigns souls to eternal fire for natural faults—an act of obvious cruelty. Thus, at the end of his opinion, he stains with plain injustice the one he had called good.

Augustine, however, as though trusting the man he addresses as his patron, is bolder. He despises his teacher’s hesitation and does not hesitate to begin where Mani ended. He pronounces that God makes and creates evil—that is, sin. This plainly cannot fit the God worshiped by the catholic faith. Let this above all remain fixed in the reader’s mind: no believer has ever had a greater cause for struggle than ours, and anyone who considers nature itself a necessity for crime has no share in worshiping the Christians’ God. Since this has often been stressed—the usefulness of the central case required repetition—let us now examine the first humans, whose indictment the Numidian carries like a light shield when he meets our battle line.

He presses into all his writings the claim that only Adam and Eve were made good by God—that is, subject to no natural guilt—and that they sinned by free will, but so greatly that they overthrew everything God had established in their nature. He says: ‘The devil planted that sin far greater and deeper than the sins familiar to people. Therefore, through that great sin of the first human, our nature was changed for the worse there, and not only became sinful but also generates sinners. Yet the very sickness through which the power of living well perished is not nature but a defect. That sin which changed the human being for the worse in paradise, because it is far greater than we can judge, is inherited by everyone born’ (compare Augustine, Marriage and Sexual Desire 2.34.57–58).

See how openly he explained his meaning! Those first humans, he says, had a good nature, but committed a sin so monstrous and immeasurable that they destroyed the power to live well, extinguished the light of free will, and established a necessity of sinning thereafter. No one born from their stock could strive toward the beauty of virtues, turn away from vices, and attain holiness.

He thinks, therefore, that praising those first humans—just two people—helps him maintain a distinction between Manichaeans and advocates of inherited sin. It is hard to encounter anything more outrageous or shameless than this opinion. Freedom of choice, he says, lost its strength once it began to exercise itself.

Let us turn to him and carefully investigate each point. You admit, do you not, that the first human was made with free will, created good by God, and polluted by no corruption of sin at the outset? Yet, though his original condition was innocent, he afterward transgressed voluntarily and imposed on everyone to be born from him an unavoidable compulsion to sin. This is certainly your doctrine, which we testify was drawn from Mani’s mud. For Mani also regards Adam’s own nature as naturally evil, although formed from the flower of the first substance and far better than those who followed.

For the present, then, we must first expose the dullness of your thinking, and then show—as we have often done already—that you never step even one foot away from the Manichaeans’ hovels and brothels. To begin with, it is utterly mad to think an act of choice was mixed into reproductive seed and the operations of wills took root in conceptions. You abolish the clearest and widest distinction between natures and pursuits, and then say the first humans’ will reproduced itself in their descendants. Everything in existence struggles against this error.

Orators’ sons never brought the elegance of their fathers’ art into their infant cries; actors’ offspring did not stretch their hands in trained gestures to accompany words; warriors’ sons did not demand a trumpet from the crowd. We may pursue examples of every kind on this pattern, all sounding together more clearly than thunder. The whole of things answers that nature has one set of boundaries, will another, and the conditions of reproductive seed cannot be penetrated by the desires of chosen pursuits. It has therefore proved a belief of the dullest, most abject stupidity to think that something admittedly voluntary was transformed into nature.

But your other claim is far, far more disgraceful: you say the capacity to act was consumed when action began. Free will is simply the capacity to sin and not to sin, subject to no compulsion on either side, but able by its own choice to stand on whichever side it wants. Yet you say that once it began to will one side, it lost the ability to choose either.

Now let us prove what we said: your doctrine differs in no respect from the Manichaeans’. There is no doubt at all that Adam’s own nature was made utterly evil if it was formed with this condition: a necessity of evil but no necessity of good. A crime, even if conceived by will, would become natural in a nature in which goodness would not become natural. Such a person is falsely said to have sinned voluntarily, since he labored under the prior disadvantage of a thoroughly evil condition. How bound to evil he was is obvious, if he was destined to be filled with inseparable guilt.

What worse substance could I find than one made so that it could fall into injustice but could not leave injustice? If it had suffered this compulsion on goodness’s side, even losing free will, it would still have brought no accusation against its author: no one would challenge him over an abundance of kindness. But when such domination is placed on evil’s side, it accuses no one more than humanity’s maker himself. Flattery from his own accusers—that is, from you—uselessly strokes a god proved the closest friend of wickedness by the ugliness of what he created.

Who can be persuaded that he did not destine the first human for crimes if he deprived him of the capacity for reform; if he gave him so twisted a mind that his own error could not displease him, leaving no return to honor and no improvement through experience; if, to prevent him ever feeling a desire to recover uprightness, he tore out the very possibility of correction? If his condition was such that a single fall cost him the power to reform for as long as he lived, he was plainly established for no other purpose than to fall. Indeed, it is more accurate to say he always lay fallen than that he fell, if he is not allowed to rise in respect of conduct.

What sort of freedom, then, was supposedly bestowed on him at first, if among two contrary qualities he received the worse as necessary and the better as changeable—indeed, if, occupied by the tyranny of guilt, he was stripped of the capacity to come to his senses? The first human’s condition was therefore utterly repulsive from the outset, if God established it so unhappily that his coming fall into crime bound him to perpetual necessity of sinning.

The alliance between you and the Manichaeans plainly endures: they by open profession and you by argument maintain that even the first human’s nature was evil. All this is full of absurdities and lies. Passing over the legions of saints, let us take the first example of righteousness after Adam’s sin: Abel’s wonderful holiness proves it. Born from sinners, he showed through the actual exercise of virtue that he did not lack the power to live well (Genesis 4:4; Hebrews 11:4). Yet, leaving these examples aside, it is useful to press the pronouncements of the party teaching inherited sin.

What do you suppose the free will you acknowledge was given to the first humans was like? Surely it meant they could change their minds: do evil or withdraw from evil, abandon or keep justice. There would therefore have been no will to sin unless the capacity to will came first. You say that after they began using their own will—that is, a movement of mind compelled by no one—they lost free will. What could be imagined more insane?

To state your argument’s force precisely: you say that what was given only for the sake of willing perished because of willing. Sin is simply an evil will. Freedom was given solely to permit the will to arise, not to compel it. Yet you say this freedom lost its condition through an act of will, so it is believed to have died through the very thing that alone proves it alive. An evil will is therefore not freedom’s fruit, but evidence of freedom. Freedom is simply the capacity for good and evil, provided they are voluntary. How, then, could it perish through the very thing for which it is shown to have been instituted, when an evil will and a good will are not freedom’s destruction but its witnesses?

The distance between proper functions and destructive crises is therefore the distance between your opinion and the meaning of free will, whose destruction you think was supplied by its own grounds for praise. What new or unforeseen thing happened when humanity sinned, to overthrow God’s arrangements? A being was made who could sin and not sin. When he sinned, he did what he ought not to have done, but what he nevertheless could do. How, then, would he lose that capacity, instituted precisely so that he could will something and could refuse what he willed (Genesis 4:4) (Hebrews 11:4)?

Next, to follow the precipices of your opinion, you argue that free will was arranged on this condition: it would lose its power as the consequence of the will that followed, and thereafter endure the necessity of the quality it chose. Attend, then, to our reply. Do you think humanity was created to suffer this necessity of the chosen quality on both sides? If someone willed good, could he thereafter not sin; and if he chose evil, could he no longer reform? Or would necessity of evil follow only the evil choice, while nothing similar happened on the good side, which would always remain exposed to the dangers of change?

Take whichever of these alternatives you please. If you say nature was made to suffer only the necessity of evil, no one will doubt that a nature assigned compulsion solely toward the worse side is being defined as utterly repulsive. Adam too is proved to have possessed an evil nature, and no shadow of a voluntary offense will remain for you to hide beneath.

But if you profess that the same consequence would have followed on goodness’s side—if he had willed good he could no longer sin—I reply: Why, then, did he sin? Why did no necessity of good make him impervious to the devil’s plots, when he is found to have obeyed God for some time before sinning? The instant the clay grew warm with the soul’s entrance, he did not immediately blaze into the desire of an evil will. Rather, we read that he was placed in paradise to cultivate and guard it and received God’s command to eat all its fruits but obediently abstain from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.

Before his wife’s body was formed from his side, he therefore remained obedient to the command, an innocent cultivator of that delightful countryside. Afterward he received the help of a companion like himself. Scripture’s truthful account emphasizes these distinctions of time. Once he saw the woman prepared for him, he served God’s command with such diligent devotion that he also informed her of the law he had received. Thus he not only kept but also proclaimed the divine command, teaching Eve reverence for the one commanding, the kind of obedience required, and the reason for fear.

That is why the woman, to whom God had given no command, resisted the devil’s approach attentively. At first she refuted the serpent’s lies. She said abstinence from all trees had not been commanded, as he invented; rather, permission to enjoy all their fruit came with a warning about just one little tree, and the fear of death was set before them as the rightful consequence for transgressors. It therefore appears that Adam kept the command for no short time. Eve too cared about devotion, although she fell through love of knowledge and divinity.

Why, then, did the justice and devotion that flourished a long time in Adam and for some time in Eve not remove their ability to do wrong, so that a necessity of good made them impervious to guilty persuasions? They were obedient for as long as they wished, yet the merit of their devotion did not cost them their ability to transgress: in the end they fell (Genesis 2–3). Therefore, even after sinning, it is clear that they could not have lost the power to reform. Here, as everywhere, you have lost everything you invented. That sin of the first humans neither created necessity for any crimes nor passed into nature, just as their previous justice neither imposed necessity for virtues nor claimed the pathways of reproductive seed (Genesis 2:7) (Genesis 2:15–17) (Genesis 2:18–23) (Genesis 3:1–6).

english: What, then, has been established? One of two alternatives is necessary. Either you acknowledge that Adam was made with a good substance, that his nature was not destroyed by a voluntary quality, and you abandon natural sin; or, if you insist as before that he is the cause of natural evils, you must pronounce him too to be of an utterly evil substance and to belong to your god—that is, yours and Mani’s.

So far I have argued as the practice of our faith required. But I will not be content with this approach alone. I shall deal generously with you and deliberately take on a role that seems to favor your teacher’s position. The purpose is to force you to attack Mani, if you disagree with him. The absence of trickery in our argument will be shown by the very fact that the advocate of inherited sin can find no way to oppose Mani. Thus the extent of your conspiracy and the mutual advantages by which you manage everything will appear when no quarrel can be stirred up between you. Let the reader keep in mind the purpose I have explained for taking this course. Now let us speak in the role we assume.

[Julian argues in an assumed Manichaean voice:] ‘Those who think this bodily formation capable of justice are completely mistaken. The lowly nature of flesh and blood opposes every good pursuit. Every stimulus, through the seduction of the senses, slides into disturbing—indeed overthrowing—the mind. Cast into this mire by some unknown misfortune, the mind loses its noble flashes of light through mixture with clay. Of itself it strives toward its own place, toward the heights, but it is crushed in an earthly prison. When it wishes to fly upward to chastity, it encounters the glue and birdlime of obscene pleasure rising from burning inward parts.

‘If it desires generous liberality, it is bound in the tightest shackles of greed, disguised as thrift. If it wishes to stand in a balanced serenity of steadfastness, it is immediately overwhelmed by a hailstorm of fear and tempests of pain. Turning bloodless before every uncertainty, it cannot remain master of its own judgment. Add the night of ignorance, whose filth surrounds it. What praiseworthy quality shall we suppose in a living being that has neither keen eyes to choose useful things nor the ability to count its shipwrecks among the storms of desires and dangers?

‘Let no one falsely claim these things happened to a substance voluntarily corrupted. The original making of the first humans is found subject to these miseries. To prove this even from Moses, whom catholics revere: the first humans experienced fear’ (Genesis 2:17)s torture, terrified by the threat of danger unless they obeyed. So far as comparison allows us to judge, we think them more fearful than their descendants, since a punishment as yet experienced by no one tormented them. Why should the threat of death shake people who did not know what harm death would bring? Mere suspicions of evils plainly troubled them. In what tranquility could a mind stand when such a bitter winter of fear disturbed it?

‘And how profound its ignorance, how harsh the condition of enduring it, when it could be freed only by transgression! It would obtain knowledge of good and evil only through an act of condemnable daring. This living being, already so blind and miserable, was made restless too by inborn desire, provoked by the beauty and sweetness of the forbidden thing. As though all this were too little to express its unhappiness, it was exposed to attack by a higher nature. Who, then, could be foolish enough to suppose any good existed where he acknowledges so many instruments of misery were established?

‘This flesh, then, of the worst condition and worst nature, displayed in those first humans what it had possessed from the beginning. The good God could not have made so evil a substance. What remains except to acknowledge one giver of the soul and another creator of creatures of clay?’ (Genesis 3:6)

Mani’s battle line, whose role I had adopted, now stands in formation. You understand what we await: whoever opposes him must demonstrate it through a consistent attack. Let your doctrine fight him, then; it will appear whether it can make even a slight movement without destroying itself. He has certainly pronounced not only that everyone born from bodily union is criminal, but that Adam himself brought the necessity of faults from the formation of his inward parts and from the dirt of the clay from which he was made. He says: ‘Flesh’s nature was harmful in the first humans. It shut in, drenched, and extinguished the very spark of mind that glimmered with the pursuit of honor. Catholics are utterly foolish: they resist sinners’ testimony and will not accept even their own evidence. They see themselves not doing the good they want but performing the evil they detest (Romans 7:19), yet think there is no necessity of evil in the flesh.’

Let the advocate of inherited sin meet these highly prejudicial claims, if he can. For now I stand as a spectator and await the outcome of your conflict. What will you answer someone swearing that nature was evil even in the first humans? Undoubtedly you will reply that God, humanity’s maker, could not create evil in what he made. Therefore, since God, who does no evil, made humans, they cannot be proved naturally evil. You have said something, and truly. But consider whether you should have said it within my hearing. I care little how forcefully you shook Mani; meanwhile you have passed entirely into my jurisdiction.

Now that you are captured, I enjoy teasing you. I greet your profession with great applause and remind you to remember it. From the dignity of its author—that is, God, who does no evil—you pronounced that his works must be affirmed good. Do you think, then, that all humans generated by the sexual union God established are made by God or by the devil? If by God, how dare you pronounce them guilty and evil, when you said the decisive proof that Adam could not have been made with an evil nature was that he was created by God, who is perfectly good?

If this is a strong argument for believing the first humans’ substance was not established guilty—precisely that God, whom we acknowledge good, created it—then the same argument remains to destroy inherited sin. It proves that everyone born from marriage cannot be created unjust, because God, whom we acknowledge good, creates them. But if, even after this, raging shamelessness persists in swearing both that infants are made by God and that they are naturally evil, these lies bring no prejudice against a catholic or our God. Yet plainly you have not attacked Mani. He gladly embraces your accusation against God, content that you have lost the argument through which you tried to establish Adam’s good condition (Genesis 2:7) (Genesis 3:5).

english: But let us not press the first part of the contest too hard. Let us allow you to proceed in your opinion and prove Adam’s nature good. You surely say: A just God would not impose a law of devotion on a human being if he knew that person suffered a necessity of sinning. If he demanded justice of will from someone he knew to possess an evil nature, he would not prove the transgressor guilty, but publicly show himself an enemy of justice. Yet the just God imposed a law on humanity and promised punishment for transgression. It is therefore established that the human being, good by nature, could sin only by will alone.

You see how sound a conclusion I have offered in your name? It is precisely the sword that flashes in catholic hands and lays waste both Manichaeans and advocates of inherited sin. But I too quickly brought in your party’s name, though for now I wanted my reply taken as yours. The solid response has therefore shaken Mani. I accompany this august reasoning with fitting praise, but notice that the oil of this praise sharpens the sword against you.

Repeat, please, what you said. ‘The just God would not impose a law on humanity if it were evil by nature. But he, being just, imposed a law. It is now clear that humanity could keep what the perfectly fair God commanded, because without the power to obey, the one commanding could never have a reasonable basis for his order.’ What a delightful little argument! Before me, with me as spectator, he establishes the goodness of the nature receiving law from the justice of the lawgiver—and does not see that before Mani feels even a small wound, he has brought destruction upon the advocates of inherited sin.

To make you understand that I seize your bloody weapons while you lie half-dead, and that your dying eyes must bear the sight of victorious truth, I will drive you onto your own weapons. [Literary echo: Virgil, Aeneid 10.462–463.] If the just God could not give Adam a law unless he knew him free to observe justice without any compulsion toward evil, then without doubt the law of later times, carrying the same weight of justice, could not have been given to people if they were born from the womb either weak for good and incapable of justice, or guilty—that is, evil. That later law was also put in writing, more extensive through multiplied provisions, more precise through distinctions, and more fearsome through increased punishment.

For just as the plea of necessity would excuse these people in every transgression, the excessive commands, uncontrolled decrees, and unjust judgments would return as a stain upon their author. Thus this second part closes in the same way as the first. Either you acknowledge that God’s justice could command only what he judged those subject to him could do—in which case the first command destroys Mani, while the later laws destroy Mani and the advocate of inherited sin together—or, if impiety abandons this argument, Mani has not suffered even a slight blow from you. With the world as witness, he will show that he is your father and leader, and that he and you have one single contest against us.

I do not know whether, now driven by lack of resources, you might attempt something so foolish and weak as saying you cannot prove by any reasons that God created Adam good, but are satisfied to believe it solely on the authority of the reading. After humanity was formed on the sixth day, it says of all creatures together: ‘God saw everything he had made, and behold, it was very good’ (Genesis 1:31). You would thus judge Adam to have been established without injustice, not because of the maker’s dignity or a weighing of his justice, but because of the testimony calling all created things well made.

Yet although this strikes Mani so lightly that he laughs, it exposes the advocate of inherited sin bound before us. We need gather no crowd of divine testimonies here. The apostle’s authority alone supplies our ruling: foreseeing this foul error, he thundered against you in lofty speech, ‘Every creature of God is good’ (1 Timothy 4:4).

If Moses’ statement that God made everything well suffices to prove the first human was formed with a good nature, and you therefore insist Adam could not have been created by God with sin because he is read to have been made good among the rest, we will answer along exactly the same lines: no one can be born with sin, because the apostle defends every creature of God as good.

What have these arguments accomplished? The choice offered you in the contest declared between you and Mani has publicly revealed what reason discovered. Once the contest was proposed, you could not hurl even one weapon at your teacher without destroying yourself. Thus it shines still more clearly that you and the Manichaeans have fused through obscene agreement into a single body of impiety. What could be more closely joined than what not even the arrival of danger can separate? In every destruction of Mani, the doctrine of inherited sin dies with him. Nothing strikes him and leaves you intact. Your principles, mysteries, and dangers are one—and you resent being called old Mani’s offspring?

See, by contrast, how real our struggle is against you and Mani, whose downfall always entangles you, and how swift our triumph over him. We immediately draw the plow of our first definition around everything he vomited out to defame God’s work. We force him to explain what he thinks sin is. It plainly is nothing other than a will seeking what justice forbids and from which it is free to abstain. Once this is established, all the thornbushes of objection that pricked bodily existence are, as the writer says, shown torn out by the roots. [Literary echo: Cicero, On Ends, Book 2.]

As for the feeling of fear and the sensation of pain, through which he thought a storm arose to shipwreck humans, they are shown not merely to compel no evil, but, when checked by a good will, to assist and carry forward justice. Who would fear judgment without fear’s warning? Who would benefit from repentant groans without the cleansing of pain and inward distress? Finally, what power would a judge’s severity have unless it punished voluntary sins by the suffering of inflicted torment?

All these things testify that sin is nothing other than a free will despising justice’s commands. Justice can stand only by reckoning as sin what it knows could freely have been avoided. Consequently, no law can count natural things as faults, and no one takes on guilt for a crime he did not himself commit while able to avoid it. This argument’s power destroys both Mani and the advocate of inherited sin, who, with all the eyes of understanding gouged out, tries to attach an act of will to reproductive seed.

But by the faithfulness of our God and of humanity! Could such monstrous inventions really have been devised, deliberately and laboriously trying to assert everything upside down? What could be more monstrous than what the Carthaginian says? Things that were natural, he says, did not endure; things adopted by choice adhered to the first formation of the bodily members.

Adam, he says, was made good and possessed natural innocence. Raised above other creatures by a special nobility, he shone with his Creator’s likeness (Genesis 1:26–27). He received free will in his created condition, to move by his own judgment in whatever direction he wished. Through the very condition of his making, which set him above the rest, he obtained the ability to approach either good or evil and withdraw from either. But because he used his independent judgment to adopt a corrupt inclination of the free mind, he overthrew all those admittedly inborn things; only sin and the necessity of sinning clung to him inseparably.
This is what I called a monstrous invention. It is an unheard-of disgrace to say: A living being was well made in whom even natural goods could be lost, while even voluntary evils clung inseparably.

Someone may say here: What then? Do you deny that the innocence in which he was created was corrupted by committing a voluntary sin? Even if committing injustice does not destroy the possibility of returning to good, it is still certain that the standing of innocence with which human life begins perishes through a fault of will. I do not deny that this is so. But what I want these examples to illuminate is this: the qualities by which we are called good and evil were made to operate under the will’s authority. This was established so firmly that even innocence, which precedes the will’s activity because of the author’s dignity and is natural, has no power to preserve itself in a resisting mind. Therefore this principle must apply far, far more strongly on evil’s side: a fault adopted voluntarily must acquire no tyranny that destroys reason.

If the good quality with which humanity was made was not unchangeable—for someone unable to vary his own movements would falsely be called free—much less could an evil quality become unchangeable in a rational being. Otherwise the principle of freedom would suffer from evil’s side a restriction that, to preserve its condition, it had not suffered even from goodness’s side.

What parasite ever flattered a boastful soldier’s strength as the advocate of inherited sin flatters the devil’s? This can be recognized by weighing their respective influences. God made the human being, handling the very material of clay with an awe-inspiring condescension, as it followed its author’s hand into human shape. The completed image stood there, still pale and cold, awaiting the breath through which it would shine and live. Then the soul, created and breathed in by the author’s most august breath, stirred the inward parts it filled. Every sense awakened to prepare for its own tasks. The entering inhabitant gave color to the inward parts, warmth to the blood, vigor to the limbs, brightness to the skin. See the work divine goodness undertook in forming and animating humanity (Genesis 2:7)!

Yet the Creator’s closeness did not abandon him once complete. He was transferred to a more delightful place; the one God had mercifully made he generously enriched. Nor, content with this, did God stop there: he enlightened him by sharing conversation. He gave him a command so that, understanding his freedom, he might see the means at hand to become closer to his Creator. The command was not stretched into many provisions, lest a multiplied law impose a burden. The prohibition of one small fruit sought evidence of devotion. Later, so that he might have a companion through whom to become a father, he was ennobled again by the touch of the hand that made him. Divine conversation continued to cherish and honor him (Genesis 2:8–25).

These divine provisions—so prolonged, so many, so great: arrangements, gifts, commands, conversations—created no necessity of good in humanity. On the other side, however, the devil, as timid as he was crafty, exchanged a few words with the woman. Those words are said to have had such power that they immediately became a natural condition—indeed, overthrew every inborn thing, created perpetual necessity of evil, and imposed the devil as lord and possessor over God’s image.

What, then, is stronger, more excellent, more magnificent than the hostile power, if with a slight conversation it accomplished what God could obtain neither by his works nor by his gifts? Plainly you stand on the side of the one whose power you proclaim so excessively. You have no share in worshiping our God, whom we acknowledge as both perfectly fair and all-powerful: ‘He is mighty, and truth surrounds him’ (Genesis 3:1–6); he humbles the proud one as a wounded man—that is, the devil and Mani, and you their followers, who slander nature to avoid admitting that you sin voluntarily. Our God, then, ‘scatters his enemies by the strength of his arm’ (Psalm 89:8, 10; LXX/Vulgate Psalm 88:9, 11) (Genesis 1:26–27). Thus neither you nor the Manichaeans could bring forward anything that the thunderbolt of his truth did not shatter (Psalm 89:8, 10).
