english: It is therefore perfectly clear that Augustine differs in nothing from his teacher. His arguments define Adam’s nature as utterly evil no less than everyone else’s. To discuss further with him what we have treated, it appears that you do not even consider the first sin the same kind as other faults. You say later ages’ crimes cannot pass into nature—for example, that children born from an embezzler, a parent-murderer, or an incestuous person are not born liable for their parents’ sins—and that no crime except that one is mixed into reproductive seed. You therefore show with complete openness that you do not consider that disobedience of the same kind as the rest.

See how brief and clear our question is. If Adam’s sin was adopted voluntarily and could become natural, why are the sins committed every day by a criminal will not piled into the deformity and prejudicial condition of reproductive seed? If these sins, no less atrocious and more numerous, cannot be implanted at birth, by what law, condition, or special privilege is that one alone claimed to be inborn? If the sins we know, which law condemns and fairness punishes, are of the same kind as the first human’s sin, committed voluntarily and punished justly, why do we not understand these from that one, or that one from these? If they cannot testify to one another, how can anyone shamelessly deny that the first transgression was of another condition—produced not by will but by natural corruption?

Finally, while maintaining inherited sin, dare to define any sin. I do not mean the first; for now take one committed today—sacrilege, a shameful act, or some evil crime. Explain the definition of these sins. You will undoubtedly say: It is a will seeking what justice forbids and from which it is free to abstain; if there were no evil will, there could be no sin. Observe how reasonably we rise against this. What dullness, what intolerable shamelessness! You define sin as nothing but a free will forbidden by justice, while the theory of natural evil lays down that there is an involuntary sin with which a human is born. Then it is not true that only what is freely committed is a fault, since there is a crime—and the greatest one—received not voluntarily but by birth.

Give back, then, the definition of sin that is friendly to catholics and does not turn aside to lodge with you even as a guest. Having relinquished it, prove that you are not a fellow soldier of those who attack substance itself with the stigma of wickedness. To gather our conclusions: either no sin will be shown voluntary if any sin is natural, or none will be natural if every sin is defined as voluntary. Consequently, either deny that sin can be born and come over to catholic faith, or, if you persist that not merely some sin but the greatest crime is received through nature without will, give your name too to Mani, whom you obey in everything.

Time urges us to move on, but indignation forces me to linger here a little. Do you dare say Adam sinned voluntarily? Where did this dream come from? ‘Because,’ you say, ‘it would have been unjust for God to count something as sin unless he knew the person was free to abstain.’ What then? Did the prince of darkness whom you worship lend him this justice for a moment, then soon demand it back and strip this god of all fairness? At the beginning he understood that nothing should be counted as sin except what could freely be avoided; afterward, through all remaining time, he knew that every newborn lacked freedom to abstain.

Finally, how do you know that the only just course in Adam’s case was to punish voluntary guilt, unless you know it unjust to charge anyone with a crime admittedly received without will? Either you will consider inherited sin just, so that it can fit God’s judgment when he charges an infant with a sin committed without any will of the infant. Then you will be forced to profess it equally just and fitting for God’s judgments to have charged Adam with a sin he knew arose not from Adam’s will but from the deformity of his substance. In that case there will be no transmission of sin: the nature condemned will not have been corrupted by its agent’s choice, but badly established from the beginning, and you will confess yourself a Manichaean.

Or, coming to your senses, you will say it would be unjust to hold Adam guilty for his nature’s faults. Then it follows irrefutably that it would be utterly wicked to judge Abel, Enoch, Noah, and the whole human race liable for original guilt. If you attach this crime of judgment to your god, he alone will remain guilty in place of everyone. It will appear, as always, that he is not the God whom we catholics worship as perfectly just in the Trinity. But if you stop accusing God, you will condemn the doctrine of Manichaean inherited sin that has pierced you until now, as though returning to life.

added_allusions.reason: Abel, Enoch, and Noah are named together as righteous examples; Hebrews presents this same sequence.

english: ‘That sin which changed the human being for the worse in paradise, because it is far greater than we can judge, is inherited by everyone born’ (Hebrews 13:4) (Augustine, Marriage and Sexual Desire 2.34.58). Who told you Adam’s sin was far greater than Cain’s? Far greater than the Sodomites’? Far more monstrous, finally, than yours and Mani’s? Certainly the history supplies no occasion for this empty claim. He had been commanded to abstain from eating the fruit of one tree. Inexperienced, unskilled, unwary, without experience of fear or an example of justice, at the woman’s suggestion he took food whose sweetness and beauty had enticed him (Genesis 3:6). Recognize here a transgression of a command.

A transgression was committed, one among the rest that sinners’ pursuits have perpetrated at different times. It was no greater than when the people of Israel ate forbidden animals (compare Leviticus 11). The cause of sin lay not in the fruit’s quality but in violating the command. What, then, did Adam do to justify your accusation that his sin exceeded human estimation? Unless perhaps, following Mani’s mysteries—he keeps his hands from plucking fruits and growing things, lest he tear a part of his god that he imagines enclosed in bark and plants—you too think Adam sinned gravely because by eating the fruit he tore your god’s substance. What madness!

‘Because that sin is far greater than we can judge,’ he says, ‘it is inherited by everyone born.’ So eating forbidden fruit was a greater crime than stabbing holy Abel out of murderous envy (Genesis 4:8); than violating the rights of guests and the order of the sexes in Sodom (Genesis 19:4–9); than sacrificing one’s children to demons even under the law (Psalm 106:37); than subjecting innocent children, aware of no exercise of will and newly made by God, to the devil’s kingdom and joining them to his deserts; than accusing God of injustice; than assigning honorable marriage to the prince of darkness; finally, than to regard infants as worse than all the ungodly, worse than all pirates, because they are born through their parents’ sexual pleasure?

I do not invent this; I draw the conclusion. You called that sin greater and weightier than all crimes, such that no guilt could equal it. And you assert that infants arrive full of this great evil, which outweighs all vices. We have therefore understood correctly: the greater the sin they share, the more they take precedence in condemnation over all criminals.
translator_notes: The web Latin omits words after “through their parents.” The missing clause is verified in the printed Latin in Patrologia Latina 45, column 1555: “voluptatem, omnibus profanis, omnibus piratis pejores putare?” The complete meaning is restored here.

english: But why should hostility toward innocence arouse indignation against you, when the insolence and fury of your obscene mouth are not restrained even by reverence for divinity? You accuse infants, but God with them; you attack innocence, but also wrong fairness; you deny truth, but accuse the one you acknowledge as your god. Consequently, although we would not lack the help of reason, the transmission of sin would collapse more than sufficiently through its advocates’ deformity.

But why do we stubbornly think only truth’s reasoning should be followed, when our enemies’ battle line relies on the very dangers of life and rises against us fortified by miseries’ support? It wants to prove the transmission of faults and punishments into reproductive seed through the shame of intercourse, the pain of childbirth, and the sweat of labor. These signs—difficult births, sweating farmers, and thorny fields—are meant to make us believe in a natural crime for which the human race is exercised by so many troubles. Some think Adam’s sin made the race mortal.

I said ‘some’ because their leader Augustine was ashamed to say this. Writing to Marcellinus, he says Adam appears to have been made mortal. Yet with his usual elegance he adds that death was the wages of iniquity (compare Romans 6:23), and pronounces that the one he admits was established mortal according to nature could not have died. Those pronouncements in Genesis which afflict Adam and Eve are therefore commonly brought against us. It is now time to discuss them.

‘The Lord God said to the serpent: Because you have done this, you are cursed beyond all cattle and all beasts upon the earth. You shall go upon your breast and belly and eat earth all the days of your life. I will put enmity between you and the woman, between your seed and her seed. She shall watch for your head, and you shall watch for her heel.
‘To the woman he said: I will greatly multiply your sorrows and your groaning. In sorrow you shall bear children; your turning shall be toward your husband, and he shall rule over you.

‘To Adam he said: Because you listened to your wife’ (Romans 6:23)s voice and ate from the tree of which I commanded you not to eat from that one alone, the earth is cursed in your works. In sorrow you shall eat from it all the days of your life. It shall produce thorns and thistles for you, and you shall eat the grass of your field. In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread until you return to the earth from which you were taken, because you are earth, and into earth you shall go’ (Genesis 3:14–19).

You take these pronouncements as evidence of inborn iniquity and proclaim that women would not have suffered pain in childbirth unless the misery of Eve’s childbearing had passed to them along with her sin. You want the punishment itself to prove sin, so that what the first woman earned through her offense cannot be felt by any woman without the same iniquity. ‘There would be no pain in the woman giving birth,’ you say, ‘unless there were sin in the child being born.’

I can scarcely measure how astonished I am in meeting these claims. Your opinion has supplied so many irritations here that I can scarcely bring myself to contest it. These objections contain more sins against understanding than syllables.
translator_notes: The Genesis quotation’s “she” and “watch for” follow Julian’s Latin wording; they are not silently replaced with another Bible version’s wording.

english: First, how insane is your very claim that childbirth pain accompanies sin! It so plainly concerns the condition of the sexes rather than punishment for crimes that all animals, stained by no sin, undergo these pangs and groans in giving birth. This shows that something found even without sin is not proof of sin.

Then you advance another, far more foolish claim. ‘A woman would not suffer pain,’ you say, ‘unless she shared in crimes.’ Yet immediately you add: ‘But this sin, for which the woman suffers, is found not in the mother but in the child being born.’ (1 Corinthians 11:3) Thus, you say, even baptized women live free from sin, yet are afflicted by the difficulties of their childbearing because of the iniquity of the children they bring forth. On this opinion, inherited sin no longer flows from mother to offspring but pours back from the newborn into the parents. If a baptized woman feels pain because iniquities are found in the infant, transmission begins to run uphill rather than downhill.

‘But she is not tormented because her son has iniquity; rather, because she herself brought it with her when she was born.’ Yet you said grace removed this evil from her. If a laboring woman’s pain adhered to sin, removing sin should have cured childbirth’s torment. Or, if this torment cannot exist without iniquity, but is still found in women after baptism, then grace has not removed their iniquity either, and baptism’s ceremony has become worthless.

But if these mysteries possessed the power and truth we believe in, not what you invent, and every sin was removed, yet the pain caused by difficult childbirth remains, it is clear that this groaning indicates nature, not fault. Even you agree it is suffered by women whom you acknowledge freed from the Manichaeans’ sin. So much is clear from examples alone. If we inspect the words of the pronouncement itself, however, it will dissolve your fog with brilliance surpassing the sun’s rays.

The woman was not told, ‘Pains will arise within you,’ or, ‘I will create groaning for you,’ as though these sensations were instituted after her fault. Rather: ‘I will greatly multiply your sorrows’ (Genesis 3:16). God shows that what he promises not to create but to multiply in the sinful person already exists in the natural order. Only existing things are multiplied. Before they exist, ‘making’ is the proper expression; calling it ‘increasing’ is premature.

Lest this seem our own point rather than truth’s, this same order of words is recorded concerning all living beings. Before humanity was made, God said: ‘Let us make humanity in our image and likeness’ (Genesis 1:26). Again concerning the woman: ‘God said: It is not good for the human to be alone; let us make him a helper like himself’ (Genesis 2:18). After they were made, however: ‘He blessed them, saying: Increase and multiply and fill the earth’ (Genesis 1:28). Before their creation he did not say ‘Let them multiply,’ but ‘Let humanity be made.’ Once someone existed who could increase, he appropriately added, ‘Increase and multiply and fill the earth.’

In this same order, childbirth’s groaning, established naturally in human bodies as in animals, was not created in Eve but increased, so that she would suffer a special intensity of heightened pangs. Yet these would reach later women only in the ordinary natural measure, varying with their bodies. Thus sin did not cause the woman to suffer in childbirth, but to suffer excessively. Similarly, we read of bodily infirmities coming upon particular people for sins at different times; but such increased misery did not overturn the smaller natural measure.

Not everything in this pronouncement, however, is confined to punitive severity. One part indicates desert, another specifies a duty. ‘I will greatly multiply your sorrows and your groaning; in sorrow you shall bear children.’ Up to this point comes punishment, earned by the person, not by nature. From here the task of the sex created second is simply described: ‘Your turning shall be toward your husband, and he shall rule over you’ (Genesis 3:16). This plainly does not concern punishment: its absence would concern fault. A woman’s submission to her husband with modest affection belongs to order, not punishment. According to the apostle, ‘the husband is the woman’s head’ (Ephesians 5:23), because ‘man was not created for woman, but woman for man’ (1 Corinthians 11:9). If she reveres her head with fitting modesty, she maintains nature’s arrangements rather than enduring sin’s torments. If she resists that order, she is guilty. Performing something whose neglect is a fault is therefore no misery.

added_allusions.reason: Multiplication of sorrows and husband’s rule.

english: Enough about the woman; let us pass to the man’s tasks. ‘To Adam he said: The earth is cursed in your works. In sorrow you shall eat from it all the days of your life. It shall produce thorns and thistles for you, and you shall eat the grass of your field. In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread until you return to the earth from which you were taken, because you are earth, and into earth you shall go’ (Genesis 3:17–19) (Genesis 4:7). Here he did not say, ‘I will multiply your thorns or your sweat’ (Genesis 1:11–12); they are spoken of as though first created then. Yet this objection is removed with no greater effort than in his wife’s case.

First, it is not the human’s seed but the soil that is cursed: ‘The earth will be cursed in your works.’ What had the fields done to deserve the insult of a curse for the sin of someone else’s will, when they certainly could inherit nothing from Adam? Was it to teach by the very sods that a curse can exist where no fault exists? If sin was in the human but the curse in the crop, plainly guilt does not always attach to loss.

If the earth is cursed to afflict the sinner, while iniquity is not located where the curse is, why could the same condition not apply even if some miseries were shown to have been imposed on our nature after the first human’s sin? It would not follow that newborns are miserable to prove them guilty. Rather, by recalling the first sin, suffering handed down could warn against evil imitation those whom it had not made guilty. The earth likewise would be shown to have endured the insult of a curse to condemn the evil of another’s will, not to generate participation in its own guilt. Unless perhaps we believe soil dearer to God than innocence, so that while he does not allow another’s crime to pollute a clod, he nevertheless permits it to condemn infancy!

The curse is directed at the earth, then, but even this is not left unexplained. The purpose of the pronouncement and the way the soil is called cursed are set out: ‘In sorrow you shall eat from it all the days of your life.’ Notice how he explains himself. The earth is called cursed not because punishment could be inflicted on it, but because this name expresses the opinion of a grieving mind. Knowing it barren because of its cultivator’s deserts, the hungry worker in his distress would blame the soil for what he had himself deserved. Afflicted, he would call it cursed. Its fertility was withheld precisely so that the transgressor should acknowledge neither nature nor earth, but his own will and person, as subject to the curse.

‘It shall produce thorns and thistles for you.’ He was not content to say, ‘It shall produce thorns and thistles,’ but added ‘for you.’ Long before, at the command, the earth had produced thorny bushes among its other plants. Now, to sting the human being, it was promised to be thornier than usual. This could chastise Adam severely: after paradise’s springs and meadows, even one bramble could offend him.

But ‘In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread’ does not seem to me especially connected with misery. Sweat is even a natural aid, refreshing the limbs of workers. The text itself testifies that cultivation’s labor lay upon him before sin: ‘The Lord God took the human he had made and placed him in paradise to work and guard it’ (Genesis 2:15). Even in paradise, then, God did not want him to receive food with absolutely no labor, but by requiring work stirred the industry he had implanted. What new thing do we believe happened if someone who experienced labor also felt sweat?

It continues: ‘Until you return to the earth from which you were taken, because you are earth, and into earth you shall go.’ This last part of the pronouncement, like the woman’s, concerns information, not punishment. Indeed, as the matter shows, it comforts the human by promising an end. Above, it had recalled pains, labors, and sweat, whose sensation nature received and whose excess the person received. Lest these seem to extend forever, the announced limit softens the distress—as though to say: You will not always suffer these things, but only until you return to the earth from which you were taken, because you are earth and into earth you shall go.

After saying, ‘Until you return to the earth from which you were taken,’ why did he not add, ‘Because you sinned and transgressed my commands’? That should have been said if bodily dissolution belonged to crimes. What did he say instead? ‘Because you are earth, and into earth you shall go.’ He showed the reason for returning to earth: ‘Because you are earth.’ The earlier words explained how he was earth: ‘Because you were taken from earth.’ If God said the reason for returning to earth was having been taken from earth, and that taking could not concern iniquity, then beyond doubt bodily dissolution in one who was not eternal belonged to mortal nature, not iniquity.

That barrenness of trees, abundance of thorns, and increased distress of painful childbirth were therefore imposed on particular people, not the race. When Cain and Abel were born, both shared one nature but had different wills. Cain, sinning voluntarily, gained nothing from the fact that his father’s sins did not burden him; Abel suffered no harm from his parents’ wrongdoing. Each, by personal judgment, through a different purpose and outcome, publicly showed that neither virtue nor vice carried a natural determination within him.

Performing priests’ work, they offered sacrifices to God their creator. Unequal care distinguished their outwardly equal service. God’s pronouncement made this clear, showing Abel’s gift pleased him. To the offended Cain he explained his displeasure: Cain had offered rightly but divided wrongly. Immediately the impious mind blazed with envy and, burdened by his brother’s holiness, gratified envy with a brother’s murder. Thus at the first occasion it became clear that death is not evil, since a righteous person was the first of all to undergo it.

Yet the guilty mind’s audacity did not escape God’s anger. Cain was questioned about his brother, convicted of his crime, and sentenced to punishment. Besides the terror laid upon him as the mark of his cruelty, he was punished by a curse from the earth: ‘You are cursed from the earth, which opened its mouth to receive your brother’s blood from your hand. When you work the earth, it shall no longer give you its strength’ (Genesis 4:3–12). See, once again the earth’s barrenness is decreed as the cultivator’s punishment. Countless kinds of torments are also threatened in Deuteronomy (Deuteronomy 28:15–68).

What then? Did the thickets in our fields, which the farmer labors to cut back with his billhook, sprout through Cain’s murder? Since you think every owner of thorny land liable for the sin punished by abundant thorns, will all infants now be said not only to have eaten fruit, though born toothless, but also to have shed Abel’s blood? The madness reached by Manichaean inherited sin is clear. Since it contains nothing but insanity, catholics’ sober judgment laughs at your arguments; yet those same people’s affection weeps over your ruin.

added_allusions.reason: Cain offered rightly but divided wrongly: Julian follows the Septuagint/Old Latin form of the verse.
The earth had already been commanded to produce plants, before the curse on Adam.

translator_notes: The statement that Cain “offered rightly but divided wrongly” follows the Septuagint/Old Latin wording of Genesis 4:7. It differs from the wording of many modern English Bibles translated from the Hebrew; Julian’s form is retained because his argument uses it.

english: What, finally, will be said about the serpent itself? Do you think that curse punished the devil or this ordinary crawling animal? The pronouncement says to the serpent: ‘You are cursed beyond all cattle and all beasts upon the earth. You shall go upon your breast and belly and eat earth all the days of your life’ (Genesis 3:14). Do you think it was fulfilled in the devil’s punishment, or in the beast that spring warmth draws out of its holes?

If in this serpent, whose form stretches into a body without joints, and if you say that fault’s desert made it an earth-eater, then inherited iniquity burdens all beasts too. You think such transmission can occur only through the desire of those coupling. It follows that you must assert the devil planted the desire of serpents and hence of irrational animals. With your position exposed, you will blare Mani’s tune at us.

But if you acknowledge that everything said to the serpent was fulfilled spiritually in the devil, you will undoubtedly agree that the punishment spoken there neither proves present-day serpents guilty nor means the devil bodily eats earth. Even if he then enlisted the serpent’s service, and fatherly severity afterward broke it like the weapon he had used to wound humanity, sin still remained solely in the agent’s will.

Foods, thorns, and sweat were first established naturally, afterward increased judicially in certain cases, and have reached our own age [without that sin itself being passed on]. These matters are so plain that they require no lengthy defense.
translator_notes: The bracketed phrase follows a reading recorded in the printed edition: Migne, PL 45, column 1576, note 2, reports Morel’s “admigratione” (passing or transmission) and also proposes “adjunctione” (attachment). The main printed text has “admiratione” (wonder or admiration), which is difficult to make sense of here. This choice is an editorial interpretation of a recorded alternative, not a certain restoration of Julian’s wording.

english: Yet lest we seem to have passed anything over carelessly, consider another point. Childbirth pain is known to vary with mothers’ bodies and strength. Women among foreign peoples and shepherds, hardened by exertion, give birth during journeys with such ease that they tend and immediately carry their offspring without interrupting the labor of travel. Not exhausted by childbirth’s difficulty, they transfer the womb’s burden to their shoulders. Generally, poor women’s lack of resources requires no midwives’ services. By contrast, wealthy women are softened by luxury: the more attendants each has, the more she learns and desires to be ill, and she thinks she needs as many services as she has available.

The hands of wealthy husbands certainly never experience the first human’s misery among thorns. Confident in their resources and placed beyond fear even of hunger by extensive estates, they consider it beneath them to spend a moment wishing for fertility. Sometimes, as the poet says, they order: ‘Unyoke the oxen, provided you send truffles’ (Genesis 3:16–19) (Juvenal, Satires 5.119).

If, then, women’s childbirth pain belongs to nature’s arrangements, as shown both by irrational animals’ example and the precise divine pronouncement; if withholding of fruit and the rise of thorns were created among other things but made denser and more troublesome for particular people; if childbirth’s difficulty and soil’s thorniness vary with bodies and regions; if the former pang continues in women’s inward parts after grace, while wealthy luxury knows nothing of the latter; and if the reason bodily dissolution would follow was expressly stated and attached to the manner of making rather than to errors—then here too everything plainly agrees with catholic truth. Neither women nor thorns help you at all.

added_allusions.reason: Continued discussion of childbirth, thorns, labor, and the return to earth.

english: I certainly will not attack those who think Adam, had he obeyed, could have been transferred to immortality as a reward. We read that Enoch and Elijah were taken away so as not to see death (Genesis 5:24; Hebrews 11:5; 2 Kings 2:11). But nature’s arrangements are one thing, rewards for obedience another. One person’s merit is not so great as to overturn everything established naturally. Inborn mortality would therefore have continued operating in the rest, even if that first human had passed from prolonged life to eternity.

This rests not on a conjecture open to denial but on a certain example: Enoch’s children could not be freed from the condition of dying by their father’s immortality. Nor should anyone perhaps object that, if not sinners, at least all the righteous would have reached immortality without intervening bodily dissolution. Abel, first among the righteous, Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and every company of saints in both Testaments displayed their merit through virtues and their nature through death.

Christ’s authority also confirmed this settled matter. The Sadducees put a question to him using a woman married seven times, asking which husband would chiefly claim her if bodily resurrection were believed. He answered: ‘You are mistaken, knowing neither the Scriptures nor God’ (Genesis 5:24)s power. In the resurrection they neither marry nor take wives, for they will not die’ (Matthew 22:29–30; Luke 20:35–36). Knowing his own work, he explained why he had instituted marriage: reproduction would make up death’s losses. Generous fertility would cease at once when grasping death ceased.

If, then, Christ who created it testifies that fertility was made to contend with frailty, and marriage’s condition was arranged before sin, mortality too plainly belongs not to transgression but to nature, to which we read marriage also belongs. The law promulgated—‘On the day you eat what is forbidden, you shall surely die’ (Genesis 2:17) (Hebrews 11:5)—therefore means penal death, not bodily death. It threatens sins, not reproductive seed; only transgression incurs it, and only reform escapes it.

Its being said to fall on the day of sin follows Scripture’s practice of calling condemned someone still to be condemned. Thus the Lord says in the Gospel: ‘Everyone who has not believed in me is already judged, because he has not believed in the name of God’ (2 Kings 2:11)s only-begotten Son’ (John 3:18). This does not mean that unbelief denying Christ was already joined to eternal punishment before the time of judgment, since everyone who comes to faith was formerly an unbeliever. Rather, to display the lawgiver’s judgment, sins are spoken of as already punishments. Finally, both the book called Wisdom and many people’s opinion affirm that Adam himself was cleansed through subsequent reform (Wisdom 10:1–2).

added_allusions.reason: Wisdom rescues the first-formed human from transgression.

english: Enough now about Genesis. Let us turn to the apostle Paul, whom Mani and the advocate of inherited sin think supports their opinion. Discussing the resurrection of the dead, he says: ‘As all die in Adam, so all will be made alive in Christ’ (1 Corinthians 15:22) (Psalm 116:15). You, with whom we have our dispute, appropriated this testimony. But because you did not say what you thought it established, I can scarcely confirm it, though I suspect it.

What does it have to do with transmission of sin if everyone is said to die in Adam, when Adam is a human being’s name, while transmission denotes sin and Manichaean corruption? Unless perhaps you acknowledge Adam himself to be and to mean nothing other than sin, so that by this name the apostle seems to have pronounced that everyone dies in sin? But this is obviously insane.

What is strange, then, if, since the Hebrew word Adam means nothing other than ‘human’—as its translation expresses—the apostle said, ‘All die in Adam, and all will be made alive in Christ’: those who die according to human nature are raised from the dead through Christ’s power? Anyone denying this statement is mad. By the power of the same author who established fertility and mortality in this life, everyone will be raised from the graves, ‘so that each may receive what belongs to deeds done in the body, according to what was done, whether good or evil’ (2 Corinthians 5:10).

In the apostle’s saying, then, ‘As all die in Adam, so all will be made alive in Christ,’ do you think he indicates bodily death, common to the just and unjust, or that penal death appointed for the devil and the ungodly? If this ordinary natural death, which in the saints is even precious (Psalm 116:15; LXX/Vulgate Psalm 115:6), and happens equally not only to good and evil people but also to humans and animals—if, I say, the apostle indicates this death—then plainly ‘Adam’ denotes human nature, while ‘Christ’ denotes the power of the Creator who raises the dead.

But if you want ‘All die in Adam’ to mean guilt rather than nature, an explanation is available as plain as it is certain: As all—that is, many—die by imitating Adam, so all—that is, many—are saved by imitating Christ. Either he spoke of common death and indicated nature, or of sin and condemned imitation. So he added shortly afterward: ‘As we have borne the image of the earthly one, let us also bear the image of the heavenly one’ (1 Corinthians 15:49). Certainly assuming the image could not be commanded if it were considered natural in either quality.

added_allusions.reason: Humans and animals share bodily death; the language closely resembles this passage.

translator_notes: The source note cites Psalm 115:5, but the wording “precious” death of the saints corresponds to Psalm 116:15, LXX/Vulgate Psalm 115:6; the navigable reference is corrected.

“Let us also bear” preserves the imperative form of 1 Corinthians 15:49 in Julian’s Latin quotation. His argument depends on its being a command. Many modern English Bibles instead read “we shall also bear.” The imperative is also retained when Julian repeats the verse in sections 39 and 40.

english: But let us examine the whole context of the passage. ‘If Christ is proclaimed as raised from the dead,’ he says, ‘how do some among you say there is no resurrection of the dead? If there is no resurrection of the dead, Christ has not risen either. If Christ has not risen, our preaching is empty and your faith is empty. We are also found false witnesses about God, because we testified against God that he raised Christ, whom he did not raise. For if the dead do not rise, Christ has not risen either. If Christ has not risen, your faith is vain, because you are still in your sins. Those who fell asleep in Christ have therefore perished too. If we hope in Christ only in this life, we are more pitiable than all people.

‘But now Christ has risen from the dead, the firstfruits of those who sleep. Since death came through a human being, resurrection of the dead also comes through a human being. For as all die in Adam, so all will be made alive in Christ. But each in his own order: Christ the firstfruits, then those who belong to Christ, at his coming; then the end’ (1 Corinthians 15:12–24).

The outstanding teacher built his argument with great force and gave us hope through our shared condition with the Mediator. He maintained that this man, as regards the substance by which he is joined to us, possessed no exemption, and that the opinion adopted by unbelief could prejudice Christ no less than us. He therefore joins Christ’s case and humanity’s so closely that what is judged in one must necessarily be believed in the other.

At that time people had thought there would be no resurrection of the dead, yet they did not deny that Christ had risen. The Teacher of the Gentiles seizes this and pronounces that both sides must be open to the same judgment: either all humans are to rise, or Christ must be believed not to have risen. The apostle certainly would not have this argumentative force if, according to the Manichaeans and their disciples who teach inherited sin, he separated Christ’s flesh from participation in our nature (1 Corinthians 15:12–17).

added_allusions.reason: Paul’s argument that denying the resurrection of the dead also denies Christ’s resurrection.

english: He would never say, ‘If the dead do not rise, Christ has not risen either,’ if someone could reply: But Christ rose exceptionally because he was born from a virgin; humans do not rise because they were born from a diabolical union. He would immediately answer: Then what was the empty point of rising, if it served neither our hope nor our instruction? What reasonable teaching or weighty example could there be if a nature unlike ours left us without both the hope of reigning with him and the power to imitate him?

The apostle’s faith stands far, very far from this opinion. Filled with the same Spirit as Peter, he knows Christ died for us to give us an example, so that we might follow his footsteps (1 Peter 2:21). Knowing that sacrifice and example were the purpose of so great a mystery, he does not hesitate to pronounce—indeed, carefully stresses—that Christ the human has reached no place from which any of us is excluded by our nature’s condition.

‘If there is no resurrection of the dead,’ he says, ‘Christ has not risen either. But if Christ has risen from the dead, how do some among you say there is no resurrection of the dead?’ (1 Corinthians 15:12–13). That is: If you acknowledge him, as human, to have possessed the same nature as ours, on what grounds do you either think resurrection occurred in him or will not occur in the rest? Having set out the conditions, he completes the judgment on every side: ‘But now Christ has risen from the dead’ (1 Corinthians 15:20); therefore there will be resurrection of the dead.

added_allusions.reason: Christ risen as basis of general resurrection.

english: Let us turn this force against inherited sin and say: If Christ, who became human, had no natural sin, how do some among you say inborn depravity rules God’s image? If evil exists in nature, Christ too, found in that same nature, is placed under the devil’s kingdom. If he is believed guilty, our preaching is empty and your faith is empty. The apostles are found false witnesses, because they testified against God that he formed his Son innocent and holy, from David’s seed according to the flesh (Romans 1:3), if the crime of cursed seed infected him. Certainly, if we hope in such a Christ, we are more pitiable than all people (compare 1 Corinthians 15:12–19).

But now Christ, no less truly human than truly God, generated from Adam’s stock, made from a woman and made under the law (Galatians 4:4), committed no sin and therefore had no sin (1 Peter 2:22). It is therefore clear that guilt belongs to will, not reproductive seed (1 Corinthians 15:12–19) (Genesis 1:26–27).

added_allusions.reason: Son from David’s seed according to flesh.
The human person as God’s image.

english: The Manichaeans are surely pierced through, both for believing natural sin and for denying flesh’s resurrection. ‘But now,’ he says, ‘Christ has risen from the dead, the firstfruits of those who sleep. Since death came through a human being, resurrection of the dead also comes through a human being’ (1 Corinthians 15:20–21) (Romans 9:11). Here the apostle speaks not of the general resurrection, which even criminals and impious people will experience, but only of those to be transferred into glory. He indicates blessed resurrection by the unqualified name ‘resurrection,’ passing over the ungodly’s rising as though, compared with it, it were no resurrection at all.

Here, then, as I said, the apostle stresses not simply resurrection, common to good and evil people, but blessed resurrection. Resurrection and the blessedness of resurrection are not the same thing, just as resurrection and the misery of resurrection are not the same. Yet because eternal blessedness does not exist without resurrection, its name also indicates the happiness that makes being raised no cause for regret.

For example, someone praising industry, strength, and diverse pursuits may wish to describe them briefly under the heading of life: calling one person’s life learned, another’s elegant, another’s energetic. This certainly does not remove the distinction, as though life were identical with industry, elegance, or strength. Living is one thing, striving another; nevertheless you cannot strive unless you live. Likewise resurrection is not identical with blessedness—there is a miserable raising of ashes—but you will not reign unless you first rise.

Bodily death and bodily resurrection therefore stand opposite each other. If every death were penal, every resurrection would also be a reward. But the resurrection of all who are assigned to eternal fire is penal; therefore death too need not be punishment, but is natural. Just as bodily death does not in every case make dying regrettable, resurrection does not in every case make returning to life delightful. The good in the latter lies in the reward of those rising, and the bitterness in the former in the burning of those punished; both follow according to deserts.

It is therefore clear that the apostle discusses not natural death but the death of criminals, made unhappy by perpetual punishment; not common resurrection but the resurrection made blessed by everlasting glory. Where he discusses persons he does not prejudice created natures. He always preserves the distinctions and broad boundaries of natures and wills, sometimes combining terms without letting confusion destroy the particular character of things.

‘Death through a human being, and resurrection of the dead through a human being’: he does not announce here that death was created by a human, but appeared in a human. Likewise he does not say resurrection was effected by a human—that is, by Christ as human—but in a human. So the same teacher says to the Philippians: ‘He became obedient to death, even death on a cross. Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name above every name’ (Philippians 2:8–9).

The apostle Peter’s assertion agrees: ‘People of Israel, listen: Jesus of Nazareth, a man approved by God among you, you killed through the hands of the wicked. God raised him, releasing the pains of the underworld.’ Again: ‘God raised this Jesus, of whom we are all witnesses’ (Acts 2:22–24, 32). There it belonged to humanity to undergo death without injury to divinity, and to divinity to raise that man from the dead. Yet what God is declared to do, Christ himself also does in the person of the Word. For he had said: ‘I have power to lay down my life, and power to take it up’ (John 10:18). Although the Son is one person, a proper distinction attributes one thing to flesh, another to divinity.

Death through a human, then, and resurrection of the dead through a human: manifested, not created. Both were established by God. But death’s condition became evident in Adam, and resurrection’s firstfruits in Christ’s person. Here, where the apostle says, ‘Death through a human,’ if you mean through his will, it concerns no nature; if through nature, it concerns no fault. He placed two human beings opposite one another, one associated with death, the other with resurrection, refusing to subordinate the second to the first.

It follows: ‘As all die in Adam, so all will be made alive in Christ’ (1 Corinthians 15:22). Does ‘All will be made alive in Christ’ include the ungodly, or refer only to believers? If to the ungodly, because everyone is made alive in Christ, no one is punished. If to believers, then not everyone is made alive in Christ’s faith, but only believers, although absolutely everyone is raised by the same power through which they were created.

If he speaks of bodily death—‘All die in Adam’—this name indicates no guilt, since Christ too is found to have died in that same Adam. The reality of resurrection would not have followed unless the reality of death came first. The apostle therefore pronounces that all die in Adam. If this death indicates nothing other than bodily dissolution, it plainly concerns no natural sin and prejudices no innocent people: they are said to die in Adam, in whom Christ also died.

But if you want ‘All die in Adam’ to concern sin of the soul—not mere death, but guilty and miserable death, followed by the punishment assigned to crimes—then neither Christ nor the saints could be in that Gehenna. It therefore prejudices no innocent people either, who possess no voluntary evil just as they possess no voluntary good, but have only this: they were made by God. We consecrate them through baptism’s rite, so that the one who made them good by creating them may make them better by renewing and adopting them. Thus the apostle’s saying, ‘As all die in Adam, so all will be made alive in Christ,’ is as far from the suspicion of Manichaean inherited sin as Christ is from sin: he possessed no iniquity, yet lacked nothing of human nature.

added_allusions.reason: All die in Adam and live in Christ.
Infants have done neither good nor evil.
Adoption associated with the baptized person’s new condition.

translator_notes: “Pains of the underworld” preserves the Latin form of Acts 2:24 quoted here. Many modern English Bibles read “pains of death”; the quotation has not been silently conformed to that wording.

english: ‘But each in his own order: Christ the firstfruits, then those who belong to Christ at his coming; then the end’ (1 Corinthians 15:23–24) (Matthew 25:34). Elsewhere the same apostle says: ‘He is the firstborn from the dead’ (Colossians 1:18) (Psalm 110:1). ‘Then those who belong to Christ’ (Psalm 8:6): that is, the saints are caught up in the clouds (1 Thessalonians 4:17). After this, the end: these will go into the eternal kingdom, while the ungodly go into eternal fire (Matthew 25:34, 41, 46).

‘When he hands over the kingdom to God the Father, when he abolishes every rule and every authority and power—for he must reign until he puts all enemies under his feet; he has subjected everything beneath his feet—the last enemy, death, will be destroyed. When he says, Everything has been subjected, this plainly excludes the one who subjected everything to him. When everything has been subjected to him, then he himself will also be subject to the one who subjected everything to him, so that God may be all in all’ (1 Corinthians 15:24–28) (Matthew 25:41).

The kingdom of God the Father means that, when the number of saints contained in his foreknowledge is complete, every dominion and all the strength of hostile power will perish. The effect of so great a mystery must be to place all justice’s enemies beneath divine feet. This will happen when eternal death sees itself destroyed and defeated by all the saints.

When all those kinds of powers have been subjected to Christ and his body through the kingdom’s manifestation, the whole glorified congregation of saints will most certainly never cease to be subject to God. The entire body worthy of the kingdom of heaven, built under Christ as head, will cling to the divine will with perfect love, so that, with every desire for faults extinguished, God may both embrace and fill everyone.

added_allusions.reason: The enemies beneath his feet, incorporated in Paul’s argument; LXX/Vulgate Psalm 109:1.
Everything subjected beneath his feet, incorporated in Paul’s argument; LXX/Vulgate Psalm 8:7.

english: ‘Otherwise,’ he says, ‘what will those baptized for the dead do, if the dead do not rise at all? Why are they baptized for them? Why do we also face danger every hour? I die daily, by the glory I have in you in the Lord. If, humanly speaking, I fought beasts at Ephesus, what does it profit me if the dead do not rise? Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die’ (1 Corinthians 15:29–32) (Colossians 3:5).

If, he says, impious unbelief shakes this hope of future glory, in which God will be all in all, and denies resurrection of the dead, what will those baptized for the dead do? From this arose some people’s error: they think the early Gospel period had a custom whereby bystanders made the profession on behalf of corpses and even washed the dead person’s limbs with baptismal water. This plainly arose from ignorance. The apostle’s phrase ‘baptized for the dead’ indicates nothing other than what he said to the Romans: ‘We were buried with him through baptism into death’ (Romans 6:4) (Isaiah 22:13).

That is: Why do we approach baptism in a spirit of putting our members to death thereafter and living wholly as dead, if there is no hope of living after death? Why, he says, do I submit to daily dangers, constantly encountering the death persecutors inflict, so that I may boast before God of your progress, if the dead do not rise? Why, humanly speaking, did I fight beasts at Ephesus—that is, endure the beastlike fury of rioters—if resurrection of the dead is still uncertain?

‘Do not be deceived: bad conversations corrupt good morals. Some have ignorance of God; I say this to your shame’ (1 Corinthians 15:33–34) (1 Corinthians 15:28). Love of sins, he says, persuades you to distrust future things. People suppose there is no judgment so that they may sin more boldly. Those denying resurrection, he says, completely fail to understand God. You therefore deny not only reward but divine power, and should be deeply ashamed. I say it to your shame that such people can be found among you.

added_allusions.reason: Let us eat and drink, tomorrow we die.
God will be all in all.

english: ‘But someone will say: How do the dead rise? In what body do they come? Fool, what you sow is not made alive unless it first dies. Not all flesh is the same: human flesh is one kind, animals’ (Daniel 12:2) another; birds’ flesh one kind, fish another. There are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies, but the glory of heavenly bodies differs from the glory of earthly bodies. The sun has one glory, the moon another, and the stars another, for star differs from star in glory. So also is the resurrection of the dead.

‘It is sown in corruption, it will rise in incorruption; sown in dishonor, it will rise in glory; sown in weakness, it will rise in power; sown an animate body, it will rise a spiritual body. Thus it is also written: The first human, Adam, became a living soul; the last Adam a life-giving spirit. The first human is from earth, earthly; the second human from heaven, heavenly. As the earthly one is, so are earthly people; as the heavenly one is, so are heavenly people. As we have borne the earthly one’s image, let us also bear the heavenly one’s image’ (1 Corinthians 15:35–49).

He masters the difficulty through examples, saying that nothing is impossible when omnipotence promises the result. Just as he commends bodily resurrection through comparison with seeds, he explains differences among those rising through the variety of creatures. Yet throughout he speaks of the blessed’s resurrection. ‘It is sown in dishonor, it will rise in glory; sown in weakness, it will rise in power; sown an animate body, it will rise a spiritual body.’ This can certainly be fulfilled only in the saints. The ungodly are raised not into glory but into everlasting disgrace, as the prophet declares (compare Jeremiah 23:40; Daniel 12:2).

Here he appropriately distinguishes nature and grace, recalling the old testimony: ‘The first human, Adam, became a living soul’ (Genesis 2:7), then adding in his own words, ‘The last Adam a life-giving spirit.’ He shows that immortality’s gifts belong to the life-giving spirit, while a soul that merely lives belongs to a nature that will one day die. Living, then, he says, is not the same as life-giving. The life-giving one bestows immortality, which he assigns to Christ; the living one enjoys life but does not exclude mortality. He distinguished the two statements for this purpose: to show Adam was made living, but not immortal, while Christ became a spirit not merely living but bestowing resurrection—glorious for his own people, everlasting for everyone.

‘But the spiritual did not come first,’ (Romans 1:3) he says; ‘the animate came first, and then the spiritual. The first human is from earth, earthly; the second human from heaven, heavenly. As we have borne the earthly one’ (Galatians 4:4)s image, let us also bear the heavenly one’s image’ (1 Corinthians 15:46–47, 49). He plainly turns to our pursuits, wanting the difference between our past and present conduct to be as great as that between mortality and immortality. ‘The first human is from earth, earthly; the second human from heaven, heavenly.’ (1 Corinthians 15:53–56) He uses the names of substances to indicate a difference of purpose.

Christ, whom he calls the heavenly human, did not bring his flesh down from heaven. He received it from David’s seed, from Adam’s seed, and within a woman from a woman’s flesh. ‘Earthly’ and ‘heavenly’ therefore refer to virtues and vices. The next words confirm it: ‘As we have borne the earthly one’s image, let us also bear the heavenly one’s image.’ So also to the Romans: ‘I speak in human terms because of your flesh’ (Isaiah 25:8)s weakness. Just as you presented your members to serve uncleanness and lawlessness toward lawlessness, now present your members to serve justice toward sanctification’ (Romans 6:19).

Following the course of his exhortation, he adds something that, unless understood, will seem to overthrow all he has said: ‘I say this, brothers: flesh and blood cannot possess God’ (Hosea 13:14)s kingdom, nor will decay possess everlasting life’ (1 Corinthians 15:50). In these very passages he has labored only to establish flesh’s resurrection, saying it would be placed in the kingdom’s glory. Now he pronounces that flesh and blood cannot possess God’s kingdom. If flesh cannot possess it and blood cannot possess it, where is the resurrection of the dead whose splendor he has been setting forth above? But, following Scripture’s usage, he calls vices, not substance, ‘flesh and blood.’

He makes this very point clear: ‘Look, I tell you a mystery: we shall all rise, but we shall not all be changed’ (1 Corinthians 15:51). The outstanding teacher understood that above he had reserved the word resurrection for future blessedness alone. Therefore, to remove ambiguity, he explains: ‘We shall all rise’—here is the common raising; ‘but we shall not all be changed’—here is the blessed’s resurrection. Change into glory is owed only to those who deserve God’s love rather than his anger.

‘In a moment,’ he says, ‘in the blink of an eye, at the last trumpet, the dead will rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed’ (1 Corinthians 15:52). Here again he turns to the saints whom that day will find in the flesh. He says that in a moment as brief as the final ending of a sound, those who had died will be raised incorruptible—that is, whole—and those found alive will be changed into glory.

‘For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal put on immortality. When this mortal has put on immortality, then the written saying will happen: Death has been swallowed up into your victory. Where, death, is your sting? Where is your victory? Death’s sting is sin, and sin’s power is the law’ (1 Corinthians 15:53–56; compare Isaiah 25:8; Hosea 13:14).

He shows, as often, that he speaks only of the saints’ resurrection. Passing over the ungodly’s raising, he pronounces it fitting that in the saints’ bodies corruptibility should be swallowed by everlasting glory. When this is fulfilled, he says, it will be possible to taunt the devil and perpetual death, which made this natural corruption seem evil. Then the saints’ joys will rebuke it, seeing that they have crushed death’s sting, and will say: ‘Where, death, is your sting? Where is your victory? Death’s sting is sin, and sin’s power is the law.’

That is: Eternal death, you had sin as a sting with which to wound deserters of justice. Had you not been armed with this sting—that is, voluntary sin—you would have harmed no one at all. You see this sin and this sting broken by faith’s strength. Our reward bears witness, the reward from which you tried to lead us away. Your sting was sin, and the power of your sin was the law, because ‘where there is no law, neither is there transgression’ (Romans 4:15).

Or, certainly, although sin was your sting, it became stronger—only in transgressors’ minds—after the death threatened by the law was brought to it. Yet the law was not given to sharpen it. ‘The law is holy, and the commandment holy, just, and good. But sin, to appear sin, produced death in me through the good, so that sin itself might become exceedingly sinful through the commandment’ (Romans 7:12–13).

This strength your sting gained through the assistance of our voluntary iniquity is now proved defeated and broken by believers’ virtues and believers’ crowns. We therefore taunt you, ‘giving thanks to our God, who gave us this victory through our Lord Jesus Christ’ (1 Corinthians 15:57).
translator_notes: “We shall all rise, but we shall not all be changed” preserves Julian’s Latin form of 1 Corinthians 15:51, which differs from the wording in many modern English Bibles.

english: In this passage Augustine thinks death’s sting is that ancient sin, failing to understand what follows: ‘Sin’s power is the law’ (1 Corinthians 15:56). He tries to identify this law as the command given to Adam. But that law was not sin’s power; it was the occasion of sin’s coming into being. Giving strength to an existing thing differs from bringing into existence what did not exist.

Eating from that tree would not have been evil if it had not been forbidden. Once forbidden and then taken through transgression, sin arose there from the encounter of prohibition and contempt. The law was not given for the purpose of wrongdoing. Nevertheless, in doing the same thing—that is, eating from the tree—the human would not have sinned, because the tree was good, unless tasting it had been forbidden by law.

What is wrong in itself—for example, murder of a parent, sacrilege, adultery—and is recognized as evil even without enacted law can rightly be said to gain strength through the law in transgressors whom prohibition makes more eager. But when an act is not wrongfully undertaken unless forbidden, the law’s occasion properly supplies its origin as sin, not its strength.

Since I have been rather lengthy here, I close this book too by reminding my reader to examine carefully and see that God’s law offers no occasion for Manichaean impiety. If any passages are thought ambiguous, let the reader not doubt that they can be explained according to the rules of truth and reason and made consistent with justice. We condemn with the same force, a force fitting God’s law, both those who say there will be no resurrection of the dead through Christ and those who equally oppose the apostle by asserting that Christ did not possess a body of our nature, thereby honoring Manichaean doctrines (Genesis 2:16–17).

added_allusions.reason: The command that forbids eating from the tree.
